Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Recovery partition XML drop: unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml written to non-Microsoft path
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Defender Offline Scan staging (MpCmdRun -offlinescan) followed by recovery partition activity · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WinRE boot trigger: reagentc /boottore or shutdown /r /o for advanced startup · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] bcdedit.exe modifying recovery sequence or WinRE boot path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Suspicious manage-bde.exe usage: BitLocker disable / unlock / protector dump · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
WinRE boot trigger: reagentc /boottore or shutdown /r /o for advanced startup AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the WinRE re-entry step from the GreatXML chain — the attacker must reach Windows Recovery Environment to bypass BitLocker after dropping unattend.xml and ReAgent.xml. Surfaces command-line invocations of reagentc /boottore and shutdown /r /o that flag a non-interactive route into WinRE. Rationale: Article-specific: 'Reboot to Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) by holding Shift while clicking Restart' — programmatic equivalents are reagentc /boottore and shutdown /r /o. Cross-checked with MITRE T1542.005 boot-process abuse and prior YellowKey (CVE-2026-45585) write-ups confirming WinRE entry as the trigger point. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/005/ • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2026-45585
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin running reagentc /info to inspect WinRE state on a help-desk ticket
  • Imaging/MDT task sequences invoking reagentc /enable after image deploy
  • User-initiated 'Restart now' from Advanced Startup UI legitimately invoking shutdown /r /o
  • OEM recovery tools (Dell Command, HP Support Assistant) staging WinRE re-entry
  • Patch Tuesday Windows Update flow triggering shutdown /r /o /t 0 after KB install
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "wuauclt.exe", "usoclient.exe", "sedlauncher.exe")) and not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("KB", "WindowsUpdate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process chain — legitimate use almost always has explorer.exe / mmc.exe / a deployment agent as parent; service-account or scripted parents are suspicious. Cross-reference the host's recent DeviceFileEvents for unattend.xml / ReAgent.xml writes to recovery paths within the last 24h. 2) Contain: if the recovery partition shows article-matching XML drops, isolate the device immediately (network containment) before reboot — once WinRE boots into the malicious unattend.xml the BitLocker volume is exposed. Force AAD/Intune compliance non-compliant. 3) Hunt: pivot on the AccountName to find other endpoints that ran reagentc /boottore in the last 30 days, then check for paired MpCmdRun -offlinescan execution and recovery-partition file writes on each.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("reagentc.exe", "shutdown.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "reagentc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/boottore", "/enable", "/disable"))
    or (FileName =~ "shutdown.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/o" and ProcessCommandLine has "/r")
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\reagentc.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\shutdown.exe"
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\reagentc.exe" and CommandLine has_any ("/boottore", "/enable", "/disable"))
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\shutdown.exe" and CommandLine has "/o" and CommandLine has "/r")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WinRE Boot Trigger via reagentc or shutdown /o
id: 9c2f1d3a-7c4b-4a91-b1a2-2e8f9b5d4f10
description: Detects command-line invocations that pivot the system into Windows Recovery Environment, a precursor used by the GreatXML BitLocker bypass.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1542.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_reagentc:
    Image|endswith: '\reagentc.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/boottore'
      - '/enable'
      - '/disable'
  selection_shutdown:
    Image|endswith: '\shutdown.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/o'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - '/r'
      - '/o'
  condition: selection_reagentc or selection_shutdown
level: medium
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) (@EventID:4688 OR @EventID:1) (@Image:(*\\reagentc.exe OR *\\Reagentc.exe OR *\\REAGENTC.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*boottore* OR *enable* OR *disable*)) OR (@Image:(*\\shutdown.exe OR *\\Shutdown.exe OR *\\SHUTDOWN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*\/o* AND *\/r*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(reagentc|shutdown)\.exe$/i
| (ImageFileName=/\\reagentc\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(boottore|\/enable|\/disable)/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\shutdown\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/\/o\b/i AND CommandLine=/\/r\b/i)
| UserName!=/\$$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=reagentc.exe OR Processes.process_name=shutdown.exe) (Processes.process="*boottore*" OR Processes.process="*/o*" OR Processes.process="*-o*") Processes.user!="*$" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=reagentc.exe OR Processes.process_name=shutdown.exe) (Processes.process="*boottore*" OR Processes.process="*/o*" OR Processes.process="*-o*") Processes.user!="*$" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Suspicious manage-bde.exe usage: BitLocker disable / unlock / protector dump AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the BitLocker tampering surface adjacent to the GreatXML bypass — manage-bde.exe being invoked with disable/unlock/protector-extraction flags, which an attacker would use to confirm or weaponise volume access after escaping into WinRE. Rationale: Article frames GreatXML as the second BitLocker bypass after YellowKey/CVE-2026-45585; manage-bde.exe is the canonical user-mode tool for inspecting/disabling BitLocker that an attacker uses post-bypass to confirm volume access or harvest protectors. Cross-checked Microsoft Learn docs for manage-bde flag set and MITRE T1552.004. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/manage-bde • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/004/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT helpdesk running 'manage-bde -protectors -get' during a recovery-key retrieval workflow
  • Asset-disposal automation disabling BitLocker before drive wipe
  • MDM / Intune compliance script auditing protector state
  • User-initiated suspend during firmware update via 'manage-bde -pause'
  • BitLocker enrollment scripts on freshly-imaged hosts running -off / -on
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("intunemanagementextension.exe", "sccmexec.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "bdesvc.exe")) and not(InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "services.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "-status")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the host has a paired ServiceNow / Intune ticket for BitLocker change; confirm the initiating account is a privileged IT user (look up AccountName in IdentityInfo). Pull DeviceFileEvents for ReAgent.xml / unattend.xml writes on the same host in the past 24h. 2) Contain: if the disable/unlock action was not change-managed, freeze the device's AAD primary refresh token, force re-enrollment, and trigger Intune compliance-non-compliant. 3) Hunt: query the past 30 days for other hosts where the same AccountName ran manage-bde with destructive flags; correlate with reagentc /boottore from UC1 to identify the full chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "manage-bde.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-off", "-disable", "-protectors -get", "-protectors -disable", "-unlock", "-pause", "-forcerecovery")
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\manage-bde.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("-off", "-disable", "-protectors -get", "-protectors -disable", "-unlock", "-pause", "-forcerecovery")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Recovery partition XML drop: unattend.xml or ReAgent.xml written to non-Microsoft path AIWeaponization High
Detects the core GreatXML payload step — writing an unattend.xml at the recovery-partition root and a ReAgent.xml under Recovery\WindowsRE. Excludes TrustedInstaller / Windows-update writers so only abnormal-origin processes alert. Rationale: Article literally names the two files and their paths: 'Copy an XML file (unattend.xml) and a recovery folder containing another XML file (Recovery/WindowsRE/ReAgent.xml) to the root of the recovery partition.' This is the most specific, alert-grade IOC in the article. Confirmed file-name semantics via Microsoft docs on Windows Recovery Environment configuration. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/deploy-windows-re • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/005/
ATT&CKT1542.005 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DISM / sysprep generating unattend.xml during in-place upgrade (filtered)
  • OEM image-restore tools rebuilding Recovery partition
  • Windows Feature Update writing ReAgent.xml via TrustedInstaller (filtered)
  • Backup software (Macrium, Veeam Agent) snapshotting recovery contents
  • Third-party BitLocker MDM agent writing recovery metadata
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and its hash — anything other than the filtered allowlist is high-confidence malicious for this article. Verify the file landed at the recovery-partition root (not C:\Windows\Panther\unattend.xml which is normal). Pull the XML content via live response and inspect for autologon credentials or RunSynchronous command lines. 2) Contain: isolate the host (network containment) before next reboot — the GreatXML chain only activates on WinRE entry, so blocking the reboot prevents BitLocker exposure. Snapshot the recovery partition for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (reagentc /boottore) and UC5 (Defender offline scan staging) timeline on the same host; expand the hunt org-wide for the same writing process hash and the writing-account UPN in the last 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "reagent.xml", "autounattend.xml")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Recovery\", @"\WindowsRE\")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "wininit.exe", "smss.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "reagent.xml", "autounattend.xml")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Recovery\", @"\WindowsRE\")
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "wininit.exe", "smss.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects writes of unattend.xml / ReAgent.xml / autounattend.xml into Recovery or WindowsRE paths by processes other than Windows servicing components — the GreatXML BitLocker bypass payload drop.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\Recovery\\* OR *\\WindowsRE\\*) @TargetFilename:(*\\unattend.xml OR *\\Unattend.xml OR *\\UNATTEND.XML OR *\\ReAgent.xml OR *\\reagent.xml OR *\\REAGENT.XML OR *\\autounattend.xml) -@Image:(*\\TrustedInstaller.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\TiWorker.exe OR *\\tiworker.exe OR *\\wininit.exe OR *\\dism.exe OR *\\sysprep.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/\\(Recovery|WindowsRE)\\.*\\(unattend|reagent|autounattend)\.xml$/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(trustedinstaller|tiworker|wininit|smss|dism|sysprep)\.exe$/i)

bcdedit.exe modifying recovery sequence or WinRE boot path AIInstallation Medium
Catches the boot-configuration tampering an attacker performs to ensure WinRE picks up the dropped ReAgent.xml / unattend.xml on the next reboot during the GreatXML bypass. Targets bcdedit /set with recoverysequence, recoveryenabled, osdevice, or {bootmgr} arguments. Rationale: GreatXML hinges on WinRE consuming the planted ReAgent.xml; bcdedit is how recovery boot pointers are realigned. Cross-checked with MITRE T1542.001 'Pre-OS Boot: System Firmware' and Microsoft bcdedit docs covering recoverysequence/recoveryenabled semantics. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/devtest/bcdedit--set • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/001/
ATT&CKT1542.001 T1542.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Update install rebooting with a transient bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy change
  • Dual-boot configuration / Linux installer adding entries
  • Macrium Reflect or Veeam recovery agent registering its boot entry
  • IT admin troubleshooting boot loop via 'bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no'
  • Enterprise imaging post-task running bcdedit to finalize osdevice
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "wuauclt.exe", "usoclient.exe", "sedlauncher.exe")) and not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("bootstatuspolicy IgnoreAllFailures", "/enum"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: collect the parent process and account — bcdedit launched from cmd.exe / powershell.exe with an interactive user is significantly more suspicious than a Windows servicing parent. Dump current BCD store via 'bcdedit /enum all' through live response and compare to baseline. 2) Contain: revert the BCD entry to known-good ('bcdedit /set {default} recoverysequence {default-recovery-guid}'), then network-isolate before next reboot. 3) Hunt: pair with UC3 (recovery XML drops) on the same DeviceId in the past 24h; if both fire, treat as confirmed GreatXML exploitation and trigger ransomware-class IR.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "bcdedit.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/set", "/create", "/copy")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("recoverysequence", "recoveryenabled", "winload", "{bootmgr}", "osdevice", "device partition", "bootstatuspolicy")
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bcdedit.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/set", "/create", "/copy")
| where CommandLine has_any ("recoverysequence", "recoveryenabled", "winload", "{bootmgr}", "osdevice", "device partition", "bootstatuspolicy")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender Offline Scan staging (MpCmdRun -offlinescan) followed by recovery partition activity AIDelivery High
Hunts the exact precondition the researcher named: 'If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're automatically vulnerable.' Detects MpCmdRun.exe -offlinescan and joins to subsequent unattend.xml / ReAgent.xml writes on the recovery partition within 24h. Rationale: The researcher literally named offline-scan as the vulnerability prerequisite: 'If you ever attempted to use Windows Defender Offline Scan, you're automatically vulnerable to a BitLocker bypass.' MpCmdRun.exe -offlinescan is the canonical Defender CLI invocation for that flow (per Microsoft Learn). Joining it to the article's exact file drops (unattend.xml + ReAgent.xml in Recovery/WindowsRE) gives a high-fidelity multi-stage alert. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/defender-endpoint/command-line-arguments-microsoft-defender-antivirus • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/new-greatxml-exploit-bypasses-windows.html
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1542.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate offline-scan run followed by Windows Update Feature Update rewriting ReAgent.xml within 24h
  • SCCM/Intune compliance baseline triggering offline scan and a separate sysprep cycle
  • User-initiated 'Microsoft Defender Offline scan' from Windows Security UI during malware cleanup that coincidentally precedes Feature Update
  • Backup snapshot capturing recovery files shortly after a legitimate scan
  • Vendor antivirus migration script invoking MpCmdRun -offlinescan during uninstall
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe", "tiworker.exe", "dism.exe", "sysprep.exe")) and not(OfflineCmd has "-removedefinitions")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the offline-scan was user-initiated (check Defender event log channel for AV-Operational EID 1000/1001 and matching MDATP scan IDs). Validate the writing process for the recovery XMLs is not TrustedInstaller / DISM. 2) Contain: network-isolate before next reboot and snapshot the recovery partition. Forcibly revert ReAgent.xml to the gold image (or run 'reagentc /disable' followed by /enable to regenerate) and clear unattend.xml. 3) Hunt: chain with UC1 (reagentc /boottore), UC3 (XML drop), and UC4 (bcdedit) on the same DeviceId — any two of these in a 24h window on the same host is high-confidence GreatXML exploitation and warrants org-wide expansion on the writing-account UPN.
let OfflineScan = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "mpcmdrun.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-offlinescan", "WdBoot")
    | project OfflineTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, OfflineCmd = ProcessCommandLine, OfflineAccount = AccountName;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Recovery\", @"\WindowsRE\")
| where FileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "reagent.xml", "autounattend.xml")
| join kind=inner OfflineScan on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (OfflineTime .. OfflineTime + 24h)
| project OfflineTime, FileDropTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, OfflineAccount, OfflineCmd,
          FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FileDropTime desc
let OfflineScan = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith "\\MpCmdRun.exe"
    | where CommandLine has_any ("-offlinescan", "WdBoot")
    | project OfflineTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, OfflineCmd = CommandLine, OfflineUser = SubjectUserName;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Recovery\", @"\WindowsRE\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("unattend.xml", "reagent.xml", "autounattend.xml")
| join kind=inner OfflineScan on $left.DvcHostname == $right.Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (OfflineTime .. OfflineTime + 24h)
| project OfflineTime, FileDropTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, OfflineUser, OfflineCmd,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by FileDropTime desc
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) ((@Image:(*\\MpCmdRun.exe OR *\\mpcmdrun.exe OR *\\MPCMDRUN.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*-offlinescan* OR *WdBoot*)) OR (@EventID:11 AND @TargetFilename:(*\\Recovery\\* OR *\\WindowsRE\\*) AND @TargetFilename:(*\\unattend.xml OR *\\ReAgent.xml OR *\\reagent.xml)))
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\MpCmdRun\.exe$/i CommandLine=/(\-offlinescan|WdBoot)/i)
| join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\(Recovery|WindowsRE)\\.*\\(unattend|reagent|autounattend)\.xml$/i}, field=aid, include=[TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, _time])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as offlineTime values(Processes.process) as offlineCmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=MpCmdRun.exe (Processes.process="*-offlinescan*" OR Processes.process="*WdBoot*") by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join dest [| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as dropTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as path values(Filesystem.file_name) as fname from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=unattend.xml OR Filesystem.file_name=ReAgent.xml) (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\WindowsRE\\*") by Filesystem.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | where dropTime >= offlineTime AND dropTime <= offlineTime+86400 | convert ctime(offlineTime) ctime(dropTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as offlineTime values(Processes.process) as offlineCmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=MpCmdRun.exe (Processes.process="*-offlinescan*" OR Processes.process="*WdBoot*") by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join dest [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as dropTime values(Filesystem.file_path) as path values(Filesystem.file_name) as fname from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name=unattend.xml OR Filesystem.file_name=ReAgent.xml) (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Recovery\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\WindowsRE\\*") by Filesystem.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`] | where dropTime >= offlineTime AND dropTime <= offlineTime+86400 | convert ctime(offlineTime) ctime(dropTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,

        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",

    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Webserver process writes PHP-executable file to public web-root or upload directory (CVE-2026-48062) AIInstallation High
Detects php-fpm, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or the php interpreter creating .php / .phar / .phtml / .phps / .pht files under common public web roots (public, webroot, htdocs, www, uploads, public_html). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass advisory explicitly warns of this landing-on-disk artefact when applications save with the original client filename via $file->move($path). Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit conditions: 'save uploads using original client filename', 'store uploads in a web-accessible directory', 'allow PHP files to run from that directory'. The webserver-account UID writing a PHP-executable extension under /public is precisely the post-validation-bypass artefact. Filename-extension list (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht) covers all PHP-handler-mapped extensions and matches the article's exact bypass example (shell.php).
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Composer install / git pull during a legitimate deploy, when the webserver UID writes vendored .php files into public/
  • CMS plugin or theme installer writing .php under public/uploads/ via an in-app admin upload (WordPress, Drupal extension store)
  • Dev environment with hot-reload writing into the document root under the webserver UID
  • CodeIgniter4 cache writers writing PHP cache shards to writable/cache (filter via the writable/ prefix)
  • Imagick or thumbnailer wrappers that legitimately move processed assets into /public/uploads/thumbs/ — if any are .php-suffixed (rare)
Suppression filter
and not (FolderPath has_any (@"\writable\","/writable/",@"\vendor\","/vendor/",@"\.git\","/.git/")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","git pull","git checkout","git clone","deploy")) and not (FileName startswith "index.php")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the file at FolderPath\FileName from a forensic copy — confirm presence of webshell strings (eval, system, base64_decode, assert, passthru) or polyglot GIF/JFIF magic followed by `<?php`. Pull the SHA256 to VirusTotal / internal sandbox. Identify the upload endpoint by tracing InitiatingProcessId backwards through DeviceProcessEvents. 2) Contain: quarantine the file (rename to .quarantine, chmod 000), block the source IP at WAF, and disable the affected CodeIgniter4 application or stop the webserver if active exploitation is ongoing. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId for outbound NetworkConnect/DnsRequest from php-fpm/w3wp in the next 24h, look for additional .php drops on neighbour hosts behind the same load balancer, and confirm CodeIgniter4 version inventory against CVE-2026-48062 (UC 4 below).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phps" or FileName endswith ".pht"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\public\", @"\webroot\", @"\htdocs\", @"\www\", @"\uploads\", @"\public_html\", "/public/", "/webroot/", "/htdocs/", "/www/", "/uploads/", "/public_html/")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileRenamed" or EventType =~ "FileModified"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","nginx","w3wp","caddy","php.exe","php")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("php","phar","phtml","phps","pht")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\public\",@"\webroot\",@"\htdocs\",@"\www\",@"\uploads\",@"\public_html\","/public/","/webroot/","/htdocs/","/www/","/uploads/","/public_html/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Webserver / PHP interpreter writes PHP-executable file to public web root (CVE-2026-48062)
id: 2c54e1a8-3b4e-4d8c-9a9a-3f7b2a1c4d6e
description: |
  Detects webserver / interpreter processes (php-fpm, php-cgi, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy, php) writing
  PHP-executable files (.php/.phar/.phtml/.phps/.pht) under common public web-roots. This is the
  landing-on-disk artefact of the CodeIgniter4 ext_in upload-validation bypass (CVE-2026-48062) where
  a file named shell.php with GIF-like content passed `ext_in[avatar,gif]`.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2gr4-ppc7-7mhx
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.008
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_process:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\php-fpm.exe'
      - '\php-cgi.exe'
      - '\httpd.exe'
      - '\nginx.exe'
      - '\w3wp.exe'
      - '\caddy.exe'
      - '\php.exe'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.php'
      - '.phar'
      - '.phtml'
      - '.phps'
      - '.pht'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\public\'
      - '\webroot\'
      - '\htdocs\'
      - '\www\'
      - '\uploads\'
      - '\public_html\'
  condition: selection_process and selection_ext and selection_path
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate composer install / git pull writing new PHP modules under public during deploy
  - CMS plugin or theme installer dropping PHP includes in public web-root
  - Developer hot-reload pushing PHP into the public dir on a non-prod host
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\php-fpm.exe OR *\\PHP-FPM.exe OR *\\php-cgi.exe OR *\\httpd.exe OR *\\HTTPD.exe OR *\\nginx.exe OR *\\Nginx.exe OR *\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.exe OR *\\caddy.exe OR *\\php.exe OR *\\PHP.exe) @TargetFilename:(*.php OR *.phar OR *.phtml OR *.phps OR *.pht) (@TargetFilename:(*\\public\\* OR *\\webroot\\* OR *\\htdocs\\* OR *\\www\\* OR *\\uploads\\* OR *\\public_html\\*) OR @TargetFilename:(*/public/* OR */webroot/* OR */htdocs/* OR */www/* OR */uploads/* OR */public_html/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/(php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|nginx|w3wp|caddy|php)\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$/i
| regex("(\\\\|/)(public|webroot|htdocs|www|uploads|public_html)(\\\\|/)", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count(as=writes))

Webserver / PHP interpreter spawns shell or LOLBin — post-upload RCE indicator AIExploitation High
Detects php-fpm, php-cgi, nginx, httpd, w3wp, caddy or php.exe directly spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash or LOLBins (whoami, net, certutil, curl, wget, bitsadmin). The CodeIgniter4 ext_in bypass culminates in arbitrary code execution when the dropped PHP file is requested — this catches the resulting child process even when the on-disk artefact is missed. Rationale: Article's stated impact is 'arbitrary code execution' via the dropped PHP file being requested by the attacker. The PHP interpreter forking a shell or recon LOLBin is the classic post-webshell-execution shape and is extremely uncommon in production PHP stacks outside of imagemagick/ffmpeg wrappers, which can be excluded via cmdline. Parent-child pair is the high-fidelity signal — neither side alone qualifies.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP applications using exec/system to call ImageMagick (convert), ffmpeg, or wkhtmltopdf — flag and allowlist by cmdline
  • WordPress / Drupal cron jobs shelling out to wp-cli or drush from php-fpm
  • Application-installed monitoring agents using whoami/hostname from PHP for diagnostics
  • Composer post-install / post-update scripts running during deploys
  • PHP-based queue workers (php-resque, Laravel Horizon) that legitimately spawn child processes for job isolation
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","ffmpeg","wkhtmltopdf","gs ","ghostscript","imagemagick","wp-cli","drush","artisan","composer")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer install","composer update","post-install","post-update"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — webshells frequently pass attacker input as the arg (e.g. 'cmd.exe /c whoami'). Pull the upstream PHP request from W3CIISLog/access logs around Timestamp ±5s using ProcessId correlation. 2) Contain: kill the PHP-FPM worker pool (systemctl restart php-fpm or iisreset), block source IP, and pull the on-disk PHP files written by that worker UID in the last 24h for analysis. 3) Hunt: enumerate further child processes from any php-fpm/w3wp in the org over the last 7d (DeviceProcessEvents | parent in PHP set), check for outbound C2 from those workers (DeviceNetworkEvents), and run UC1 to find the webshell artefact.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm.exe","php-cgi.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","w3wp.exe","caddy.exe","php.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh.exe","bash.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","reg.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","systeminfo.exe","tasklist.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\php-fpm.exe","\\php-cgi.exe","\\httpd.exe","\\nginx.exe","\\w3wp.exe","\\caddy.exe","\\php.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\curl.exe","\\wget.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\reg.exe","\\hostname.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\tasklist.exe")

HTTP multipart upload: image Content-Type with PHP/executable filename extension (CVE-2026-48062 exploit shape) AIDelivery High
Detects the exact bypass condition described in the advisory at the request layer: a multipart upload where the Content-Type header indicates an image (image/gif, image/png, image/jpeg) but the multipart filename ends in .php / .phtml / .phar / .phps. CodeIgniter4's pre-4.7.3 ext_in rule trusts the MIME-guessed extension and accepts the file. Requires WAF or application-level HTTP body parsing — IIS / Apache access logs alone do not expose multipart filenames. Rationale: Article names the exact rule: `ext_in[avatar,gif]` is bypassed by `shell.php` containing GIF-like content. The detectable signature at ingress is the multipart-part mismatch: declared Content-Type=image/* AND filename=*.php. WAF / app-tier HTTP logging is required (IIS/Apache plain access logs don't expose multipart filenames), so falcon_logscale_query and defender_kql are intentionally empty — FDR and Defender DeviceNetworkEvents don't carry decoded multipart part headers.
ATT&CKT1190 T1036.008
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentest / red-team running automated file-upload bypass tests against the same endpoint
  • Bug-bounty researcher submitting test payloads via a known WAF-allowed source IP
  • Misconfigured client uploading a .php file that the client incorrectly tagged as image/jpeg (rare, usually a browser-side bug)
  • WAF replay/debug traffic from QA environment that has been mirrored into the prod log stream
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP in ("<pentest-egress-ip>","<bug-bounty-egress-ip>")) and not (UA has_any ("Burp","sqlmap","OWASP ZAP") and SourceIP startswith "10.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full multipart body from the WAF and confirm whether the file was accepted by the upload endpoint (HTTP 200/302 vs 4xx). Identify the target CodeIgniter4 host(s) and the resolved file path on disk by tracing the SrcIpAddr to backend logs. 2) Contain: block SourceIP at the WAF, drop any uploaded artefact from disk after preserving a forensic copy, and verify CodeIgniter4 framework version >= 4.7.3 on the receiving app. 3) Hunt: search the prior 30d of WAF logs for the same SrcIpAddr against any upload endpoint org-wide, and pivot to UC1 / UC2 to see whether the dropped file was executed.
let UploadEndpoints = dynamic(["/upload","/avatar","/uploads","/file","/profile","/image","/photo","/picture"]);
let ImageMimes = dynamic(["image/gif","image/jpeg","image/jpg","image/png","image/webp","image/bmp","gif","jpeg","png","jpg","webp","bmp"]);
union isfuzzy=true

    CommonSecurityLog

    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | where RequestURL has_any (UploadEndpoints)
    | where FileType in~ (ImageMimes)
    | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(php|phar|phtml|phps|pht)$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestHost=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, FileName, FileType, UA=RequestClientApplication
),
(
    ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
    | where Url has_any (UploadEndpoints)
    | where FileMimeType in~ (ImageMimes)

    | project TimeGenerated, Vendor=EventVendor, SourceIP=SrcIpAddr, DestHost=HttpHostName, RequestURL=Url, RequestMethod=HttpMethod, FileName, FileType=FileMimeType, UA=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable CodeIgniter4 framework inventory (CVE-2026-48062, < 4.7.3) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-state hunt: enumerates hosts where Defender TVM or Sentinel inventory reports composer:codeigniter4/framework at a version < 4.7.3, scoped by the CVE-2026-48062 advisory. Use this to drive patch deployment and prioritise application-layer monitoring for the run-time detections in UC1-UC3. Rationale: Pure inventory pivot using the CVE explicitly named in the advisory (CVE-2026-48062) and the affected package `composer:codeigniter4/framework` < 4.7.2. Sigma omitted because asset-state inventory is not a single-event-shape detection. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch omitted because composer-level framework inventory is not in their standard schemas — Defender TVM and Sentinel TVM are the canonical surfaces.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts with CodeIgniter4 vendored under a non-production path (CI runner image, archived backup) which is not actively served
  • Container hosts whose TVM scan reports the package inside a stopped image layer rather than a running container
  • Dev-only laptops with cloned codeigniter4/CodeIgniter4 git source for contributor work
  • Vendored CodeIgniter4 inside a parent application that ships its own patched fork (rare — verify with the app team)
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-reference each DeviceName with the CMDB to identify owning team, application name, and exposure (internet-facing vs internal). Prioritise IsInternetFacing=true. 2) Contain: open a change ticket to upgrade composer:codeigniter4/framework to >= 4.7.3, and for any host that cannot patch within 72h apply the advisory's listed workarounds (move uploads outside webroot, use $file->store() or $file->move($path, $file->getRandomName()), disable PHP execution in upload dirs). 3) Hunt: enable UC1/UC2/UC3 alerting on the affected hosts and review the prior 30d of WAF logs against any upload endpoints those apps expose.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m

| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010

| where EventID == 4663

| where Account !endswith "$"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or SHA1 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68") or MD5 in~ ("22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["22b38dad7da097ea03aa28d0614164cd25fafeb1383dbc15047e34c8050f6f67", "078163d5c16f64caa5a14784323fd51451b8c831c73396b967b4e35e6879937b", "fe1033335a045c696c900d435119d210361966e2fb5cd1ba3382608cfa2c8e68"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phantom Gyp: small binding.gyp written into node_modules during npm install · [LLM] Editor/AI tool auto-execute config file dropped into project tree by package manager or git
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] VS Code/Cursor/Claude/Gemini spawns interpreter referencing folderOpen or SessionStart hook script · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Miasma and Hades Are Spreading Now: Detect Them on Developer Machines with Suspi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint · [LLM] Hades on-import payload: python interpreter spawns Bun runtime download · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Bun runtime egress to npm/PyPI publish endpoints or attacker-controlled GitHub repos
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Miasma/Hades known-bad SHA256 execution on developer endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts when any of the 5 SHA256 hashes associated with the Miasma/Hades June 2026 campaign are observed as either an executed binary or a file written to disk on an enrolled host. Catches the worm landing or running irrespective of the delivery vector (npm install, IDE folder open, PyPI import). Rationale: Uses the 5 SHA256 IOCs pre-extracted from the StepSecurity advisory. Cross-checked against Semgrep's Miasma v2 writeup and StepSecurity's Hades campaign writeup which confirm the same hash family. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/binding-gyp-npm-supply-chain-attack-spreads-like-worm • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/the-hades-campaign-pypi-packages • https://semgrep.dev/blog/2026/miasma-v2-self-spreading-npm-worm-now-uses-malicious-bindinggyp-file-and-compromises-57-packages/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating IOC in a sandbox VM enrolled to production tenant
  • Defender threat-intel sample auto-downloaded to MpCmdRun quarantine folder
  • Forensic analyst copying the sample to a triage share for review
  • SOAR enrichment pipeline storing the binary in an evidence bucket synced back to disk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Scans\" and FolderPath !has "\\Quarantine\\" and FolderPath !has "\\evidence\\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the host's last 24h DeviceProcessEvents/DeviceFileEvents and confirm whether the hash was executed (process row) or only landed (file row). Identify the parent (npm.exe, node-gyp, python.exe) and the originating package/folder path. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the device in Defender (Isolate Device), force-rotate any npm/PyPI/GitHub/AWS/GCP/Azure tokens that lived on that host or in any repo the developer recently opened — assume tokens were exfiltrated. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on AccountUpn across all hosts for the same hash, then hunt UC2/UC3 (Phantom Gyp + Hades Bun) against the same user/devices to map full scope; review GitHub for any new workflow files or attacker-controlled repos.
let MiasmaHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);

let MiasmaHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe","e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d","c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c","7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655","b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
