npm publish / login / auth-token write from a developer endpoint AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces npm auth and publish CLI activity plus .npmrc credential-file writes on workstations - the precursor to a package-hijack supply-chain attack. Splits the original (broken) single-column lookup into a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents so neither query references a non-canonical column. Rationale: Article frames npm install as the supply-chain risk, but credential write + publish from a developer endpoint is how a package gets hijacked at source. Hunts for npm publish/login/token CLI flows and .npmrc credential-file writes (which carry _authToken=). Uses canonical Defender columns only - replaces the previous query that referenced a non-existent NpmrcWrites column with a clean union of DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceFileEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/configuring-npm/npmrc
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal package authors running npm publish to a private registry as part of normal workflow
  • Onboarding flows that create ~/.npmrc with corporate registry tokens
  • CI agents publishing release artifacts on tag push
  • Developers running npm whoami / npm login after rotating their npm token
  • IDE plugins (VS Code, JetBrains) writing project-local .npmrc files
Suppression filter
| where not (Initiator has_any ("actions-runner","gitlab-runner","TeamCity","Jenkins","agent.exe") and EventKind == "npm_auth_cli")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user is an authorized package publisher; for .npmrc writes, read the file and look for _authToken=, registry overrides, or always-auth=true on non-corporate hosts. 2) Contain: if unauthorized publish, immediately revoke the npm token (npm token revoke) and the user's npmjs.com session; if a malicious package version was published, contact npm security to deprecate/unpublish and notify downstream consumers. 3) Hunt: pivot on the username across npm registry audit logs for prior publishes; check whether the same .npmrc token appears on other endpoints; look for outbound POSTs to registry.npmjs.org/_token or /-/v1/login from the same host in the last 24h.
let NpmAuth = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=ProcessCommandLine, Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
let NpmrcChange = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=strcat(FolderPath,"\\",FileName), Initiator=InitiatingProcessFileName;
NpmAuth
| union NpmrcChange
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd")
| where CommandLine has_any ("npm publish","npm login","npm adduser","npm token create","npm token revoke","npm whoami")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, EventKind="npm_auth_cli", Details=CommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName =~ ".npmrc"
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, EventKind="npmrc_write", Details=TargetFilePath)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm install with --ignore-scripts=false or NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS override AIWeaponization High
Catches explicit attempts to re-enable lifecycle scripts that npm 12 disables by default - via --ignore-scripts=false CLI flag, NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false env var, or the new approve-scripts opt-in path. After the v12 upgrade rolls out, an adversary with code-exec on a developer box needs to flip this back on to land lifecycle-based persistence. Rationale: Article explicitly names --ignore-scripts as the flag npm 12's new default replaces, and references npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as the opt-in. NPM_CONFIG_* envvar form is documented npm config behavior. After the v12 ramp, any of these strings on a developer endpoint is an adversary opting out of the new default. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html • https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v10/using-npm/config
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers running npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending as instructed by the GitHub blog during upgrade prep
  • Build scripts that legitimately set NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false for native-module builds
  • Dockerfile RUN lines that force --foreground-scripts for log visibility
  • Internal tooling that wraps npm and passes the flag through transparently
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "allow-scripts-pending" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName endswith "\\explorer.exe" and AccountName has_any ("dev","engineer","build"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user, package set, and whether this was the documented upgrade-prep approve-scripts flow vs a fresh install with the flag flipped. Pull surrounding child processes within +/- 60s. 2) Contain: if not approved, isolate the host and capture node_modules for the project; revoke any tokens present in .npmrc. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for the same flag pattern in the last 30 days, look for the same flag combined with --registry pointing off-mainstream, and check whether the same user/host hit UC1 (lifecycle-script suspicious child) in the same window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","npm.cmd")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\npm.cmd") or ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("--ignore-scripts=false","--ignore-scripts false","ignore-scripts=false","NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false","--foreground-scripts","allow-scripts-pending")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm install re-enables lifecycle scripts via --ignore-scripts=false or env override
id: 5e6f7a8b-9c0d-4e1f-2a3b-4c5d6e7f8a9b
description: Detects explicit re-enabling of npm lifecycle scripts after npm 12 disables them by default - via CLI flag, env var, or approve-scripts opt-in.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/github-to-disable-npm-install-scripts.html
author: SOC
date: 2026/06/12
tags:
  - attack.t1562.001
  - attack.t1195.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.cmd'
  selection_flag:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--ignore-scripts=false'
      - '--ignore-scripts false'
      - 'ignore-scripts=false'
      - 'NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false'
      - '--foreground-scripts'
      - 'allow-scripts-pending'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_flag
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.cmd) @CommandLine:(*"--ignore-scripts=false"* OR *"--ignore-scripts false"* OR *"ignore-scripts=false"* OR *"NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS=false"* OR *--foreground-scripts* OR *allow-scripts-pending*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/^.*\\(npm(\.exe|\.cmd)?|node\.exe)$/i
| regex("(--ignore-scripts(=|\\s+)false|ignore-scripts\\s*=\\s*false|NPM_CONFIG_IGNORE_SCRIPTS\\s*=\\s*false|--foreground-scripts|allow-scripts-pending)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count())

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

| order by conn_count desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is

    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:

            - 'invoke-expression'

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation

    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-10520 — Ivanti Sentry OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-06-11 1 use case 1 technique 2 kill-chain phases detected

Ivanti Sentry (formerly known as MobileIron Sentry) contains an OS command injection vulnerability which could allow a remote unauthenticated user to achieve root-level remote code execution. This vulnerability can be successfully exploited in cases where the Sentry appliance is in an unmanaged state with its endpoints externally reachable. The use of mTLS with EPMM or restricted HTTPS access through Neurons for MDM makes interfaces inaccessible to external actors. Vendor: Ivanti, Product: Sentry. Federal patch due: 2026-06-14.

Installation of vulnerable Baileys WhatsApp library (CVE-2026-48063) AIWeaponization Medium
Detects npm/yarn/pnpm installation of the Baileys library at versions vulnerable to remote message-upsert / history-sync / app-state spoofing via crafted protocolMessage payload (baileys or @whiskeysockets/baileys < 6.7.22, or >= 7.0.0-rc.1 < 7.0.0-rc.12). Hunts the supply-chain footprint since the exploit itself is purely application-layer and not visible to EDR. Rationale: Pivots on the only concrete strings in the advisory: package names `baileys` / `@whiskeysockets/baileys` and the exact vulnerable version ranges (`< 6.7.22`, `7.0.0-rc.1..rc.11`). Command-line regex captures the resolved version and tags it `yes-v6` / `yes-v7rc` / `check-manually` so analysts can triage without a separate lookup. Deliberately keeps `node.exe` in scope to catch `node /path/npm-cli.js install baileys` invocations that bypass the npm shim. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qvv5-jq5g-4cgg • https://github.com/WhiskeySockets/Baileys/commit/3beb08eecfcb4e65722e674034bd84fb11a9de35
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer or CI runner installing the patched version (baileys@6.7.22 or @whiskeysockets/baileys@7.0.0-rc12+) — will tag 'version-not-on-cmdline' or won't match the vuln regex but the row will still surface
  • Legitimate developer reinstalling all dependencies from a lockfile that pins a vulnerable version (genuine vuln, but expected hit pattern in a dev fleet)
  • Docker image build steps running 'npm install' inside a node-based container where Baileys is a transitive dependency
  • Security researcher or detection engineer doing a deliberate reproduction install on a sandbox VM
  • Yarn/pnpm running `npm i` as a wrapped subprocess on package-lock migration
Suppression filter
// Suppress confirmed-patched installs once analysts have validated the row
| where Vulnerable != "version-not-on-cmdline"
| where not (BaileysVersion startswith "6.7." and toint(extract(@"^6\.7\.(\d+)", 1, BaileysVersion)) >= 22)
| where not (BaileysVersion startswith "7.0.0-rc" and toint(extract(@"^7\.0\.0-rc\.?(\d+)", 1, BaileysVersion)) >= 12)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the matched DeviceName + AccountName, confirm whether the host is a developer workstation, build agent, or production server. Read package.json / package-lock.json on the host and confirm the resolved baileys version. If it's >=6.7.22 or >=7.0.0-rc12 the install is benign — close. 2) Contain: if the resolved version is in the vulnerable range AND the host is internet-exposed (production WhatsApp bot, customer-messaging service), engage the application owner to upgrade and apply the documented workaround (`shouldSyncHistoryMessage: () => false` and drop `messages.upsert` events containing a `requestId` field) until patched. 3) Hunt: search the same fleet for other Node.js services that import baileys/@whiskeysockets/baileys (file-event writes naming `baileys` under `node_modules/`), and check git history for any commit that reverts a Baileys upgrade — supply-chain persistence pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install "," add "," i baileys"," i @whiskeysockets","--save","--save-exact")
| extend BaileysPkg = extract(@"(?i)((?:@whiskeysockets/)?baileys)@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| extend BaileysVersion = extract(@"(?i)(?:@whiskeysockets/)?baileys@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| extend Vulnerable = case(
    BaileysVersion matches regex @"^6\.([0-6]\.[0-9]+|7\.([0-9]|1[0-9]|2[01])$)", "yes-v6",
    BaileysVersion matches regex @"^7\.0\.0-rc\.?([1-9]|1[01])$", "yes-v7rc",
    isnotempty(BaileysVersion), "check-manually",
    "version-not-on-cmdline")
| where Vulnerable != "version-not-on-cmdline"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, BaileysPkg, BaileysVersion, Vulnerable, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
let VulnV6 = @"^6\.([0-6]\.[0-9]+|7\.([0-9]|1[0-9]|2[01])$)";
let VulnV7rc = @"^7\.0\.0-rc\.?([1-9]|1[01])$";
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
     or TargetProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","node.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "baileys" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "baileys"
| extend CmdLine = coalesce(TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where CmdLine has_any ("install "," add "," i baileys"," i @whiskeysockets","--save","--save-exact")
| extend BaileysPkg = extract(@"(?i)((?:@whiskeysockets/)?baileys)@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, CmdLine)
| extend BaileysVersion = extract(@"(?i)(?:@whiskeysockets/)?baileys@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, CmdLine)
| extend Vulnerable = case(
    BaileysVersion matches regex VulnV6, "yes-v6",
    BaileysVersion matches regex VulnV7rc, "yes-v7rc",
    isnotempty(BaileysVersion), "check-manually",
    "version-not-on-cmdline")
| where Vulnerable != "version-not-on-cmdline"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, CmdLine, BaileysPkg, BaileysVersion, Vulnerable
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| BaileysVersion := regex_extract("(?i)(?:@whiskeysockets/)?baileys@([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", field=CommandLine, group=1)

    BaileysVersion=* | Vulnerable := "check-manually";
    * | Vulnerable := "version-not-on-cmdline"
  }
| Vulnerable!="version-not-on-cmdline"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, BaileysVersion, Vulnerable], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=lastSeen), collect([CommandLine], multival=true, separator=" | ")])

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiClient EMS service spawning shell or downloader (JDY post-exploit of CVE-2026-35616) · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] MIPS architecture-aware shell-script dropper on Linux (JDY botnet stage 1)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to Tor relay ports from non-Tor process (JDY C2 channel) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] High-volume mixed-protocol scanning fan-out from internal host (JDY scanning bot behaviour) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
FortiClient EMS service spawning shell or downloader (JDY post-exploit of CVE-2026-35616) AIExploitation High
Detects post-exploit behaviour from JDY botnet's weaponisation of CVE-2026-35616 against Fortinet FortiClient EMS. The EMS daemon/service has no legitimate need to spawn cmd, PowerShell, bitsadmin, certutil, curl or wget — when it does, that's the unauthenticated-RCE foothold being used to stage the next stage of the JDY shell-script dropper. Rationale: Black Lotus Labs reported a sharp spike in JDY scans against Fortinet devices within hours of CVE-2026-35616's April 5, 2026 disclosure; the EMS service binaries (FCTDas.exe, FortiClientEMS.exe) have no legitimate reason to spawn interpreters or downloaders, so this pivot has near-zero baseline. Corroborated via Lumen blog, watchTowr advisory and Tenable write-up identifying CVE-2026-35616 as FortiClient EMS 7.4.5-7.4.6 improper-access-control unauth RCE. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://watchtowr.com/resources/fortinet-forticlient-ems-zero-day-cve-2026-35616-active-exploitation-underway/ • https://www.tenable.com/blog/cve-2026-35616-fortinet-forticlientems-improper-access-control-vulnerability-exploited-in-the • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-35616
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Fortinet TAC engineer launching cmd.exe via remote troubleshooting session against the EMS host
  • Scheduled task under SYSTEM that legitimately invokes PowerShell for FortiClient endpoint inventory queries
  • Software-deployment tooling (SCCM, Intune) querying EMS via PowerShell as SYSTEM
  • FortiClient EMS upgrade routine that legitimately invokes bitsadmin/certutil to download a hotfix from a configured Fortinet URL
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("FortiClient_Update","\\Fortinet\\FortiClient\\Update\\") and InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm whether the EMS host is internet-exposed (public IP / firewall rule for TCP/8013 or 443). Pull the child cmdline + any outbound connections from the EMS host within 5 min of the spawn. Check the FortiClient EMS version — vulnerable range is 7.4.5-7.4.6 (hotfix or 7.4.7 required). 2) CONTAIN: isolate the EMS host; rotate any enrolment tokens / service-account creds stored in EMS; if a shell-dropper artefact landed, snapshot it before terminating the process tree. 3) HUNT: pivot on the child SHA256 across the estate; query DeviceFileEvents for files written by FCTDas.exe in the last 30 days; check outbound from the EMS host to Tor relay ports (9001/9030/9050) or residential-ASN IPs — both are JDY infrastructure tells.
// JDY post-exploit of CVE-2026-35616 — FortiClient EMS service launching an interpreter / downloader
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("FCTDas.exe","FortiClientEMS.exe","fcEMS.exe","FortiClient.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"Fortinet\FortiClientEMS"
| where FileName in~ (
    "cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe",
    "certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe",
    "regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe"
  )
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// JDY post-exploit of CVE-2026-35616 via Windows EID 4688
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\FCTDas.exe"
     or ParentProcessName endswith @"\FortiClientEMS.exe"
     or ParentProcessName endswith @"\fcEMS.exe"
     or ParentProcessName has @"\Fortinet\FortiClientEMS\"
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
     or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe"
     or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
     or NewProcessName endswith @"\bitsadmin.exe"
     or NewProcessName endswith @"\certutil.exe"
     or NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"

     or NewProcessName endswith @"\mshta.exe"

     or NewProcessName endswith @"\rundll32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MIPS architecture-aware shell-script dropper on Linux (JDY botnet stage 1) AIInstallation High
Detects the JDY botnet's initial dropper pattern: a shell-spawned wget/curl/tftp invocation referencing one of the article's named MIPS architecture suffixes (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64). JDY's shell script probes the host and selects an architecture-matched payload; matching that token in a downloader cmdline is high-signal on Linux endpoints/build hosts where MDE-Linux or FDR-Linux is present. Rationale: Article literally names the four architecture variants — mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64 — that the dropper selects between, making token-match on a shell-spawned downloader cmdline very high fidelity. Corroborated by Lumen blog and SecurityAffairs JDY write-up. Drops the noise floor by restricting the parent to bona-fide shell binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://securityaffairs.com/193490/malware/jdy-botnet-evolves-after-kv-takedown-targets-military-networks.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenWrt / LEDE firmware build farms fetching MIPS toolchains or rootfs images
  • Yocto / Buildroot CI runners pulling prebuilt MIPS test artefacts
  • Embedded-systems engineering lab where developers wget MIPS test payloads to a workbench host
  • Cross-compiler validation hosts running `apt-get install gcc-mips-linux-gnu` and pulling matching test binaries
  • Docker BuildKit multi-arch image build pulling mips binaries for an emulated layer
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("build-","ci-","jenkins-","gitlab-runner-","buildkit-") or AccountName in~ ("jenkins","buildbot","gitlab-runner","yocto"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: capture the full wget/curl URL; resolve the C2 host and look it up in VT / abuse.ch ThreatFox / OTX. Tag-check the originating asset: is it a build/CI host (allowed) or general-purpose Linux/edge device (suspicious)? 2) CONTAIN: SIGKILL the parent shell PID; quarantine the dropped artefact in /tmp /var/tmp /dev/shm; sinkhole the C2 hostname at the resolver. 3) HUNT: pivot on the C2 IP/host across DeviceNetworkEvents for the past 7d; check FileWritten events for elf binaries with no extension written by the same shell; review DeviceProcessEvents for a self-delete pattern (file written by the dropper then unlinked by the same process — article notes 'Once the malware is launched, it's deleted from disk').
// JDY shell-script dropper: wget/curl/tftp pulling an architecture-matched MIPS binary
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","ash","dash","busybox")
| where FileName in~ ("wget","curl","tftp","ftpget","busybox")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)(\s|/|\.|$)"
     or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)\b"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd  = ProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
// JDY MIPS dropper — ASIM cross-vendor view
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DvcOs has "Linux"
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","ash","dash","busybox")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("wget","curl","tftp","ftpget","busybox")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)\b"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet MIPS Architecture-Aware Shell Dropper
id: b7c3d4e5-f6a7-4b8c-9d0e-1f2a3b4c5d6e
description: Shell-spawned wget/curl/tftp/busybox invocation referencing MIPS/MIPSEL/MIPS64 architecture suffixes — the JDY botnet shell dropper pattern that selects an architecture-matched payload after compromise of a SOHO/IoT host.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
  - https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/ash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/busybox'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/wget'
      - '/curl'
      - '/tftp'
      - '/ftpget'
      - '/busybox'
  selection_arch:
    CommandLine|re|i: '\b(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)\b'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_arch
falsepositives:
  - OpenWrt/LEDE firmware build hosts pulling MIPS toolchains
  - Embedded-systems CI/CD pulling MIPS test binaries
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:wget OR @process.name:curl OR @process.name:tftp OR @process.name:ftpget OR @process.name:busybox) (@process.command_line:*mipsel64* OR @process.command_line:*mips64* OR @process.command_line:*mipsel* OR @process.command_line:*\.mips* OR @process.command_line:*MIPSEL* OR @process.command_line:*MIPS64*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(bash|sh|ash|dash|busybox)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(wget|curl|tftp|ftpget|busybox)$/i
| regex("(?i)\\b(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)\\b", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdline from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("bash","sh","ash","dash","busybox") AND Processes.process_name IN ("wget","curl","tftp","ftpget","busybox") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(cmdline, "(?i)(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b|\.(mips|mipsel|mips64|mipsel64)\b") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
High-volume mixed-protocol scanning fan-out from internal host (JDY scanning bot behaviour) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects when an internal device behaves like a JDY botnet scanner — one host opening connections to hundreds of distinct public IPs across many ports and a mix of transport protocols (TCP / UDP / ICMP) in a short window. This is the article's described 'high-volume TCP, SSL, UDP, and ICMP-assisted probing' viewed from inside your perimeter, catching SOHO/IoT/edge devices on your network that have been recruited into JDY. Rationale: Article describes JDY scanning as 'high-volume TCP, SSL, UDP, and ICMP-assisted probing' against 'exposed services at scale' — the distinct-IP/distinct-port + protocol-mix signature matches this profile from the inside. The 200-IP / 10-port / 2-protocol thresholds derive from the article's description and align with empirical SOHO-bot observations from Black Lotus Labs. Sigma is intentionally blank because this is a counts/threshold detection, not single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/
ATT&CKT1595.001 T1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised vulnerability scanner (Tenable Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM) running a daily perimeter sweep from an allow-listed scanner VM
  • Red-team / pentest engagement using nmap or masscan from a known jump host
  • CDN edge node or web crawler legitimately fetching from many destinations
  • VoIP/SIP gateway placing high call volumes to many external carriers
  • Backup / replication appliance pushing to many object-storage endpoints across regions
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("qualys-scanner","tenable-scanner","nessus-scanner","rapid7-scanner","pentest-jumpbox") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nmap","nmap.exe","masscan","masscan.exe","zmap","zmap.exe","rustscan"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the originating host's asset tag — confirm it is NOT on the authorised-scanner allowlist. Pull the InitiatingProcessFileName / SHA256; check whether it's a legit browser/agent or an unfamiliar binary. If the host is a SOHO/IoT class device (router, NVR, IP camera, WAP), assume compromise. 2) CONTAIN: network-isolate the host at the switchport; for endpoint-class hosts capture memory + disk artefacts before re-image. For SOHO/IoT, unplug and physically replace — JDY persistence on embedded devices is hard to clean in-place. 3) HUNT: pivot on the most-hit destination ports for 7 days to see whether other internal hosts are showing the same fan-out; check DnsEvents for DGA/fast-flux queries from the same source; review FileWritten/AsepValueUpdate on the host for the JDY MIPS-dropper artefact in the prior 24h.
// JDY bot behaviour: one internal host -> many external IPs, many ports, mixed protocols
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize DistinctIPs   = dcount(RemoteIP),
            DistinctPorts = dcount(RemotePort),
            Protocols     = make_set(Protocol),
            ConnCount     = count(),
            FirstSeen     = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen      = max(Timestamp),
            SamplePorts   = make_set(RemotePort, 25)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where DistinctIPs   >= 200     // article: 'high-volume...probing' at scale
| where DistinctPorts >= 10
| where array_length(Protocols) >= 2
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          DistinctIPs, DistinctPorts, Protocols, ConnCount, SamplePorts
| order by DistinctIPs desc
// JDY scanning fan-out — ASIM ImNetworkSession
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10."
    and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
    and not (DstIpAddr matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
| summarize DistinctIPs   = dcount(DstIpAddr),
            DistinctPorts = dcount(DstPortNumber),
            Protocols     = make_set(NetworkProtocol),
            ConnCount     = count(),
            FirstSeen     = min(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| where DistinctIPs >= 200
    and DistinctPorts >= 10
    and array_length(Protocols) >= 2
| order by DistinctIPs desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 10.0.0.0/8) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 172.16.0.0/12) -CIDR(@DestinationIp, 192.168.0.0/16)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=0
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(as=Connections), count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctIPs), count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true, as=DistinctPorts)])
| DistinctIPs >= 200
| DistinctPorts >= 10
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as DistinctIPs, dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) as DistinctPorts, values(All_Traffic.transport) as Protocols, count as Connections, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND NOT (All_Traffic.dest_ip="10.0.0.0/8" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="172.16.0.0/12" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="192.168.0.0/16") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.src | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where DistinctIPs >= 200 AND DistinctPorts >= 10 AND mvcount(Protocols) >= 2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | sort 0 - DistinctIPs
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as DistinctIPs, dc(All_Traffic.dest_port) as DistinctPorts, values(All_Traffic.transport) as Protocols, count as Connections, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND NOT (All_Traffic.dest_ip="10.0.0.0/8" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="172.16.0.0/12" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="192.168.0.0/16") by All_Traffic.src_ip All_Traffic.src | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where DistinctIPs >= 200 AND DistinctPorts >= 10 AND mvcount(Protocols) >= 2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | sort 0 - DistinctIPs
Outbound connection to Tor relay ports from non-Tor process (JDY C2 channel) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects internal hosts initiating outbound TCP connections to canonical Tor relay/SOCKS ports (9001 ORPort, 9030 DirPort, 9050/9051/9150 SOCKS) from processes that aren't Tor Browser or an authorised Tor client. The article explicitly states 'the operators use Tor nodes to manage infected infrastructure, including both the command-and-control (C2) and payload servers' — this query surfaces the JDY C2 channel emerging from a compromised host on your network. Rationale: Article explicitly states the operators 'use Tor nodes to manage infected infrastructure, including both the command-and-control (C2) and payload servers'. Tor relay ports (9001 ORPort / 9030 DirPort / 9050/9051/9150 SOCKS) initiated from a non-Tor-Browser binary is a textbook covert-channel signal. Confirmed via Lumen Black Lotus Labs report. Cross-checked against: • https://www.lumen.com/blog/en-us/expanded-jdy-iot-and-soho-botnet-enables-rapid-vulnerability-exploitation
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001 T1008
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised researcher / threat-intel analyst running Tor Browser (binary renamed for OPSEC)
  • Developer testing a SOCKS5 client against a local Tor instance for a privacy feature
  • Snowflake / Tor pluggable-transport browser extension on a user laptop
  • OnionShare being used by the SOC team for evidence transfer
  • Cryptominer / unauthorized proxy app embedded in shareware on a user-owned device
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("researcher-tor","redteam-jumpbox","opsec-vm") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--tor-research-authorized")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: extract InitiatingProcessFileName + SHA256 and look it up on VirusTotal; check whether the host is a SOHO/IoT class device or a managed endpoint. Pull prior-7d connections from the same host to the same destination — first-seen-now vs ongoing changes the urgency. 2) CONTAIN: kill the offending process; block the destination IP at the egress firewall; if the host is an embedded/IoT class device (router, NVR, IP camera, edge appliance), isolate at the switchport and physically replace — in-place clean is unreliable for JDY. 3) HUNT: query the past 7d of DeviceNetworkEvents for the same destination IP across the estate; cross-pivot to ScriptControlScanInfo / DeviceProcessEvents on the host for the MIPS-dropper pattern from UC2; check whether this host also shows the high-fan-out scanning behaviour from UC3 — same host hitting both is JDY-conclusive.
// JDY C2 channel: outbound to Tor relay ports from a non-Tor process
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 9051, 9150)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (
    "tor.exe","torbrowser.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","onionshare.exe"
  )
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
// JDY Tor C2 — ASIM ImNetworkSession
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DstPortNumber in (9001, 9030, 9050, 9051, 9150)
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10."
    and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
    and not (DstIpAddr matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr,
          DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to Tor Relay Ports (JDY C2 Channel)
id: c9d4e5f6-a7b8-4c9d-0e1f-2a3b4c5d6e7f
description: Outbound TCP connection to commonly-used Tor relay/SOCKS ports from a process that is not Tor Browser or an authorised Tor client — JDY botnet's C2 layer routes through Tor.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:(9001 OR 9030 OR 9050 OR 9051 OR 9150) -@Image:(*\\tor.exe OR *\\Tor.exe OR *\\torbrowser.exe OR *\\TorBrowser.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\Brave.exe OR *\\onionshare.exe)

| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(tor|torbrowser|firefox|brave|onionshare)\.exe$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-35616")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

Ivanti, Fortinet, and SAP Release Patches for Multiple Critical Vulnerabilities

The Hacker News
2026-06-10 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Fortinet, Ivanti, and SAP have released security updates to address multiple critical security vulnerabilities that could result in arbitrary code execution and information disclosure. The security flaw patched by Fortinet relates to a command injection vulnerability in FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI. It's tracked as CVE-2026-25089 (CVSS score: 9.1). "An

CVEsCVE-2026-25089 CVE-2026-10520 CVE-2026-10523 CVE-2026-44748 CVE-2026-27671 CVE-2026-22732 CVE-2026-40128
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1204.004 T1528

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Unpatched Ivanti Sentry / FortiSandbox / SAP NetWeaver assets — CVE-2026-{25089,10520,10523,44748,27671,22732,40128} inventory · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 exploit attempt against /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage · [LLM] FortiSandbox CVE-2026-25089 WEB UI unauthenticated command-injection probe · [LLM] SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP CVE-2026-27671 RFC kernel memory-corruption crash signal · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10523 unauthenticated admin account creation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10520 exploit attempt against /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the watchTowr-disclosed Ivanti Sentry endpoint that handleExecute() routes into the MICS configuration command path. Any external POST to this URI before the R10.5.2/R10.6.2/R10.7.1 patch is shipped is overwhelmingly likely to be exploitation, since the legitimate UI redirects unauth users to a login page post-patch. Rationale: watchTowr-disclosed URI `/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage` and the `handleExecute()` backend are quoted directly from the article body. The patch redirects unauth requests to login, so any hit on this path from a non-admin source is high-fidelity exploit traffic.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Nessus/Qualys) probing the endpoint for CVE-2026-10520
  • Ivanti professional services or partner support running post-patch verification
  • Authenticated MobileIron admins legitimately reaching the configuration UI
  • Penetration test engagements scoped against MobileIron Sentry
Suppression filter
| where Sentinel CommonSecurityLog: and SourceIP !in (<authorized_scanner_ips>)
// W3CIISLog: | where cIP !in (<authorized_scanner_ips>) and csUserAgent !startswith "Nessus" and csUserAgent !startswith "Qualys"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Confirm the source IP is not your authorized vuln scanner (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) or red team. Pull the full HTTP body if your WAF/proxy captures it — look for shell metacharacters (`|`,`;`,`&&`,backticks) or `$()` in MICS config fields. Step 2 — Contain: If the Sentry appliance is on R10.5.x/R10.6.x pre-R10.7.1, block the source IP at perimeter and pull appliance from MDM traffic until patched. Snapshot the appliance for IR. Step 3 — Hunt: On the Sentry host check for new SSH keys in /root/.ssh, modified /etc/passwd, outbound connections to non-corporate IPs, and reverse-shell processes spawned by the Tomcat/Java service. Pivot to AAD/Okta for any MobileIron-managed device that may have had its config silently tampered.
// Defender doesn't see inbound HTTP to appliances; the only Defender pivot is post-exploit outbound from Sentry hosts.
let IvantiSentryDevices = DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where DeviceName has_any ("sentry","mics","mobileiron") or RegistryDeviceTag has "Ivanti" | distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (IvantiSentryDevices)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("java","java.exe","updateagent","yum","dnf","apt-get")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
// Primary: appliance/WAF/load-balancer syslog through CommonSecurityLog.
let Window = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where RequestURL has "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome, Message
| union (
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where csUriStem =~ "/mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, scStatus
  )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ivanti Sentry CVE-2026-10523 unauthenticated admin account creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for net-new administrative accounts appearing on Ivanti Sentry (formerly MobileIron Sentry) where no authenticated session existed — the signature of the auth-bypass bug that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker mint admin accounts. The detection joins admin-creation events against a baseline of legitimate admin provisioning sessions. Rationale: Article quotes the watchTowr summary stating the patch "added authentication" in front of the vulnerable endpoint; the bug class (CVE-2026-10523) is described as letting an unauthenticated attacker "create arbitrary administrative accounts." Net-new admin accounts on Sentry without a preceding authenticated session is the directly observable downstream effect.
ATT&CKT1078.001 T1136.001 T1190
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate provisioning of break-glass admin accounts by Sentry administrators
  • Disaster-recovery restore of an old configuration snapshot that re-introduces named admin accounts
  • Ivanti professional services performing post-patch validation
  • Automation/IaC that maintains a baseline admin set
Suppression filter
| where NewAccount !in (<break_glass_account_names>) and SyslogMessage !contains "automation-bot"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the new admin's username, IP that created it, and whether any human admin session existed on the appliance within ±60s of creation. Check the appliance audit log for the preceding HTTP request — if it hit /mics/api/v2/sentry/mics-config/handleMessage or any unauthenticated endpoint, treat as confirmed CVE-2026-10523. Step 2 — Contain: Disable the new admin account, rotate all known-good admin credentials, and force re-auth on all active sessions. Block the source IP at perimeter. Step 3 — Hunt: Pull every action that new admin took (config changes, certificate exports, downstream device pushes), and review managed devices for malicious MDM configuration pushes (rogue VPN, root CA install, MDM-pushed apps). Treat any device that synced after the admin was created as potentially compromised.
// Visible to Defender only if Sentry creates a downstream AD account on a domain-joined connector.
IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in~ ("Account created","User account created")
| where DeviceName has_any ("sentry","mics","mobileiron") or Application has_any ("sentry","mobileiron")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, TargetAccountDisplayName, TargetAccountUpn, AccountUpn, IPAddress, DeviceName, Application
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 14d;
let SentryHosts = dynamic(["sentry","mics","mobileiron"]);
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where Computer has_any (SentryHosts) or HostName has_any (SentryHosts)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("admin user created","role=ROLE_ADMIN","new administrator","useradd","adduser")
   and SyslogMessage has_any ("admin","administrator","root")
| extend NewAccount = extract(@"user[=\s:]+([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, HostName, ProcessName, NewAccount, SyslogMessage
| join kind=leftanti (
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(60d) .. ago(Window))
    | where Computer has_any (SentryHosts) or HostName has_any (SentryHosts)
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("admin user created","role=ROLE_ADMIN")
    | extend NewAccount = extract(@"user[=\s:]+([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | distinct NewAccount
  ) on NewAccount
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:ivanti OR source:mobileiron OR source:syslog) ("admin user created" OR "role=ROLE_ADMIN" OR "new administrator") @host:(*sentry* OR *mics* OR *mobileiron*)

FortiSandbox CVE-2026-25089 WEB UI unauthenticated command-injection probe AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP requests to the FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI containing shell metacharacters and command-substitution patterns indicative of CVE-2026-25089 (CWE-78 OS command injection) exploit attempts against affected 5.0.0–5.0.5 and 4.4.0–4.4.8 builds. Rationale: Article explicitly names FortiSandbox / FortiSandbox Cloud / FortiSandbox PaaS WEB UI and CWE-78 OS command injection via crafted HTTP requests. With no specific URI from Fortinet's advisory in the article body, we hunt on the bug class — shell metacharacters in HTTP requests targeting the named products.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners probing FortiSandbox
  • Fortinet TAC / professional services running diagnostics
  • URI query params that legitimately contain `|` for OR-filters in search UIs
  • WAF testing scripts in a staging environment
Suppression filter
// Drop authorized scanners: | where SourceIP !in (<scanner_ips>) and RequestClientApplication !startswith "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !startswith "Qualys"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Confirm source IP isn't an authorized scanner. Decode percent-encoded request bodies and look for the actual injected command (id, whoami, curl, wget, bash, /bin/sh). Step 2 — Contain: If unpatched (FortiSandbox <5.0.6 or <4.4.9), restrict WEB UI to a management VLAN at the perimeter firewall and patch within 24h. Snapshot the appliance. Step 3 — Hunt: On the FortiSandbox host, check for unexpected outbound to non-FortiGuard IPs, new SSH keys, cron jobs, modified web-UI files, and reverse-shell processes. Validate sandbox verdicts emitted in the last 30 days for any tampering.
// Defender has no native FortiSandbox WEB UI telemetry; pivot via outbound-from-appliance reachability if FortiSandbox sensors talk to Defender-monitored hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("fortisandbox","fsa-") or RemotePort in (443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe","wget.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","java.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (";","|","$(","`","%3B","%7C","%24%28")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let Window = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where DeviceProduct has_any ("FortiSandbox","Fortinet")
   or DestinationHostName has "fortisandbox"
   or DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where RequestURL has_any (";","|","%3B","%7C","%24%28","%60","$(","`","&&","%26%26")
   or Message has_any (";rm ","|nc ","|bash","|sh ","wget http","curl http","$(id)","$(whoami)")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP CVE-2026-27671 RFC kernel memory-corruption crash signal AIExploitation Low
Hunts for SAP work-process (disp+work) crashes, segmentation faults, or kernel restart entries in the SAP application server log — the observable side-effect of an unauthenticated attacker sending a crafted RFC request that triggers the CVE-2026-27671 memory-corruption bug in the SAP kernel RFC protocol validator. Rationale: Article states CVE-2026-27671 is an unauthenticated memory-corruption in how the SAP kernel validates the RFC protocol. The exploit's observable signature is the SAP work-process crashing — disp+work / gwrd / rfcexec process termination plus SIGSEGV / 'core dumped' / 'abnormal termination' strings in the host log are direct artefacts.
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine SAP transport / kernel patch deployments causing planned restarts
  • SAP Basis admins running disp+work recycle during troubleshooting
  • Hardware faults / OOM kills unrelated to RFC traffic
  • ABAP dumps from buggy custom Z-programs
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: | where SyslogMessage !contains "kernel patch installation" and Computer !in (<scheduled_kernel_upgrade_hosts>)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull dev_w* trace files from /usr/sap/<SID>/D<inst>/work/ for the crashed work-process — look for stack trace involving CsiRfcReceive, ThRFCMsg, or ab_RfcInputHandler around the crash time. Cross-check whether SAP Note (KB equivalent of CVE-2026-27671) is applied. Step 2 — Contain: Block external/untrusted source IPs from RFC gateway ports (33xx/48xx/sapdp/sapgw) at perimeter. Apply the SAP Security Patch Day note. If kernel cannot be patched immediately, restrict gwrd via secinfo / reginfo ACLs. Step 3 — Hunt: Look for repeat crashes from the same upstream IP, post-crash creation of background SAP users, RFC-destination changes, and any successful SAP_ALL / SAP_NEW role assignments after a crash.
// Windows-hosted SAP: track disp+work / gwrd unexpected exits.
let Window = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Window)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("disp+work.exe","gwrd.exe","rfcexec.exe")
   or FileName in~ ("disp+work.exe","gwrd.exe","rfcexec.exe")
| where ActionType in ("ProcessCreated")
| summarize StartCount = count() by DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where StartCount > 2   // legit disp+work restarts are infrequent; multiple within 30m suggests crash-loop
| order by Timestamp desc
| union (
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(Window)
  | where ActionType in~ ("ApplicationCrash","ProcessTerminated")
  | where FileName in~ ("disp+work.exe","gwrd.exe","rfcexec.exe")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, AdditionalFields
)
let Window = 7d;
let SapCrashes = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName has_any ("disp+work.EXE","gwrd.EXE","rfcexec.EXE")
    | summarize Restarts = count() by Computer, NewProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
    | where Restarts > 2;
SapCrashes
| union (
    Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("disp+work","gwrd","rfcexec")
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("segfault","core dumped","signal 11","SIGSEGV","abnormal termination","ABAP-Kernel","R3_KERNEL")
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
  )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:sap OR source:linux.syslog OR source:windows.security) (@process.name:(disp+work.EXE OR "disp+work" OR gwrd OR gwrd.EXE OR rfcexec OR rfcexec.EXE)) AND (@message:("segfault" OR "core dumped" OR SIGSEGV OR "abnormal termination" OR "signal 11" OR "ABAP-Kernel"))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(disp\+work|gwrd|rfcexec)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName], function=count(as=Restarts))
| Restarts > 2
